verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Jaipur carpet exporters with verified US order books and tight monthly stock-and-receivable reporting; avoid small hand-knotted units selling into the domestic festive trade on unsecured limits.
title: Jaipur Carpets & Rugs: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A Jaipur carpet unit buys wool, silk, viscose, jute and acrylic yarn, puts it out to hand-knotters or tufting machines, and sells finished rugs into two very different channels: export buyers (the US is the visible one) and the domestic heritage/hotel/festive trade. **Cash sits in the loom, not in the showroom** — a hand-knotted piece takes months to make, so working capital is locked in work-in-progress and yarn long before an invoice exists. That is a wide price ladder, and pricing power lives only at the top of it. ## Where value and cash actually sit
**The exporter's cash cycle is order-driven; the domestic seller's is season-driven.** Jaipur Rugs' shipment records show repeated US-bound consignments of hand-knotted wool, wool-silk, tufted acrylic and viscose rugs through JNPT to Savannah [3] — so for exporters, receivables and shipping documents are the real collateral, not the loom. Domestic demand peaks before Diwali [2], which means festive stock is bought on credit and must convert within weeks. Rating evidence on a carpet peer shows the failure mode: working capital limits around 80% utilised for twelve months with cash of Rs 0.22 crore [10]. **So when a proposal lands, check limit utilisation for the last twelve months, not the last quarter; if it is above 80% through a full year, ask what the peak season does to it.**

## What has changed now
Rajasthan is running behind the country: GST collections -4.7% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, and electricity demand +4.0% against India +9.5% [D]. **That is a local demand signal, and it argues for lending to order-backed exporters rather than to units dependent on Rajasthani retail.** Nationally, carpet-and-rug output (NIC 13) is +13.1% YoY and +11.9% Apr-to-date [D], so the trade itself is not shrinking. Peer results are mixed and mostly old: Oriental Weavers' 9M 2024 shows revenue +34% with EBITDA margin 16.6% [4], while Faze Three's FY26 revenue rose 32.92% to Rs 932.76 crore but operating profit fell 20.15% [5]. **Growth without margin is the pattern to underwrite against — ask for gross margin by product line, and if tufted machine-made is carrying the growth, price the limit for commodity risk.**

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
Pursue mid-sized Jaipur exporters with confirmed US/UK purchase orders, a mix of hand-knotted and tufted, and a clean stock statement; Welspun Living's October 2026 call still expects US demand intact and targets double-digit UK revenue growth [6]. Avoid small units whose entire book is festive domestic stock and whose security is a godown of unsold rugs. **Structure as packing credit against orders plus a receivable discount, not a plain cash credit.** Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, quarterly limit-utilisation data, and shipping-bill copies per consignment. Note that this city has thin published coverage — the local sources are trade colour [1][2] and shipment data [3], not audited financials — so lean on first principles and the peer set. ## Early-warning signs
- **Limit utilisation above 80% for two straight quarters [10] -> freeze enhancement and ask for receivables ageing.**
- **US shipment frequency falling month-on-month [3] -> reprice or reduce the limit.**
- **Festive stock still unsold by December [2] -> demand inventory write-down plan before renewing.**
- **Revenue growing while operating profit falls, as at Faze Three [5] -> cut tenor and raise margin.
